Subject: DPA follow-up: operator carve-out and transient cache questions

Hi Tessa,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — the performance looked promising and the pilot team is keen to move. Procurement ran the DPA through our checklist and surfaced two technical/legal items we need clarified before we can sign:

1) Operator carve-out: your team previously described an "operator" carveout for on-call support that may access ephemeral data in certain failure scenarios. We need specifics on what data would be accessible, for how long, and assurances about scope (e.g., no persistent copies, no export outside the US without notice).

2) Transient cache / prefix KV: we use a third-party vendor to route requests (and some of our prompts include PHI-ish identifiers). Please confirm whether Redwood's transient cache or prefix caching could result in any customer data being written to non-redwood vendor systems or third-party telemetry (and if so, which subprocessors).

Can you send proposed DPA wording (redline) covering: operator access limitations, onshore fallback/offshore restrictions, short retention for transient caches, encryption-in-transit/backups, and a subprocessor roster with residency details? Procurement needs the roster + a SOC2 attestation to run the purchase order.

Attachments: our procurement checklist (attached).

Thanks,
Elena Ruiz
Sr. Procurement Manager
GreenHealth

Subject: Re: DPA follow-up: operator carve-out and transient cache questions

Elena —

Appreciate the clear list. High-level answers first, then next steps:

- Operator carve-out: Redwood operations only use an operator access path for emergency debugging or failover; access is session-scoped, time-boxed (max 2 hours by default, longer only with written justification), logged, and strictly limited to the minimum data needed to reproduce the issue. We do not take persistent snapshots; when we capture logs for triage they are redacted and retained only for the incident retention window (30 days) unless a customer asks us to keep them longer for legal or investigatory reasons.

- Transient cache: our prefix/KV cache is in-memory on our serving fleet; under normal operation nothing is written to third-party systems. We do use partner-managed monitoring agents for metrics that receive anonymized telemetry (no request payload). Subprocessors that can see telemetry or logs are listed in the roster below and we can add residency filters for your pilot.

Next steps I propose:
1) Laura (cc'd) will produce a short redline draft covering an operator-access section, an explicit transient-cache clause, and an onshore-fallback commitment for pilot customers.
2) I'll share our subprocessor roster and SOC2 link; we can mark vendors subject to onshore-only handling for GreenHealth in a schedule.
3) If that looks good, we can route a limited PO and pilot contract this week and provide SOC2 + attestation on execution.

I'll attach the initial redline and the roster; Laura, can you take the lead on language? Irene, do we need legal review or can we proceed with the redline as-is for procurement review?

Best,
Tessa Morgan
Head of Enterprise Ops (Sales)
Redwood Inference

Team —

Per Tessa's ask, I drafted a suggested redline and a short plain-language summary for the PO. Key points I added (see attached redline):
- Operator access: add explicit "purpose-limited" language, require prior written request from the customer owner except in true emergency, session recording and 2-person review for any data extraction, and automated deletion within 30 days.
- Transient cache clause: state that prefix/KV caches are in-memory and not persisted; any diagnostic dump requires customer authorization and is limited to <48 hours retention and US-residency for pilot.
- Subprocessor residency: include a Schedule A with a filtered roster for GreenHealth labeling vendors that will process pilot data and their locations.

I recommend we:
1) Share the attached redline and the plain-language PO summary with Elena today.
2) Provide the SOC2 link and a short attestation letter from Redwood security.
3) Limit the pilot schedule to US-only for storage/diagnostic dumps; operations telemetry can remain anonymized and cross-region.

If legal wants stronger wording (e.g., absolute prohibition on exports), we should be prepared to offer an onshore-only fallback with a pricing uplift.

Laura Bennett
Sr. Manager, Contracts & Privacy
Redwood Inference
